item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
Edited for Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice, .

Startups operate in unique organizational contexts characterized by resource constraints, rapid growth, uncertainty, and dynamic change. These distinctive features shape how startups attract, develop, and retain talent, creating workforce challenges and opportunities that differ significantly from established organizations.

The startup workforce represents a critical yet understudied area of organizational research. While entrepreneurship literature has traditionally focused on founders and venture capital, the employees who join startups and contribute to their success deserve greater scholarly attention. Understanding startup employment practices, workforce composition, and employee experiences provides important insights into contemporary work arrangements and organizational dynamics.

This special issue seeks papers that examine all aspects of the startup workforce, including recruitment strategies, retention mechanisms, organizational culture, compensation approaches, employee well-being, team dynamics, diversity considerations, and the experiences of workers in early-stage ventures. We welcome empirical studies, theoretical contributions, and practical insights that advance our knowledge of how startups build and manage their human capital.

Research on startup workforces has implications for multiple stakeholder groups including startup founders and managers seeking to build effective teams, employees considering careers in startups, policymakers designing support for entrepreneurial ecosystems, and scholars interested in organizational behavior and human resource management in non-traditional contexts.

Potential topics

  • Hiring and recruitment in startups
  • Employee retention and turnover in startups
  • Compensation and benefits in startup environments
  • Organizational culture and dynamics in early-stage companies
  • Leadership and management styles in startups
  • Skills development and training in startups
  • Diversity and inclusion in startup workforces
  • Remote work and distributed teams in startups
  • Employee motivation and engagement in startups
  • Career trajectories and job transitions in startup contexts
  • Human resource practices and policies in startups
  • Entrepreneurial teams and co-founder dynamics

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
This special issue aims to explore the multifaceted dimensions of workforce dynamics, human resource management, and employment relationships within startup organizations. Startups present unique organizational contexts that differ significantly from established corporations in terms of resource constraints, growth trajectories, organizational structures, and employment practices.

Potential topics

  • Employment relationships in startups
  • Work organization and management practices in startup contexts
  • Workforce diversity and inclusion in startups
  • Entrepreneurship and human resource management
  • Employee motivation and retention in startups
  • Organizational culture in startup environments
  • Skills development and training in startups
  • Labor market dynamics and startup employment
  • Remote work and flexible arrangements in startups
  • Founder-employee relationships
  • Work-life balance in startup settings

item.title: From Human Resource Management (HRM) to Artificial Intelligence Management (AIM)? — Algorithms and the Changing Governance of People at Work
item.content:encoded:
This special issue explores the fundamental shift from traditional Human Resource Management (HRM) to Artificial Intelligence Management (AIM), examining how algorithms are reshaping the governance of people at work. As organizations increasingly deploy algorithmic systems to manage recruitment, performance evaluation, scheduling, and other HR functions, we need to critically understand the implications for workers, organizations, and society.

The collection seeks to bring together diverse perspectives on how algorithms are transforming workplace governance, the mechanisms through which algorithmic management operates, and the consequences for employment relationships, worker agency, and organizational practices. We welcome contributions that examine both the promises and perils of algorithmic management across different sectors, geographies, and worker populations.

Potential topics

  • AI and algorithmic management in organizational contexts
  • The role of algorithms in HR decision-making and workforce management
  • Transformation of HR practices through artificial intelligence
  • Governance of people at work in the age of algorithms
  • Impact of AI on employment relationships and worker autonomy
  • Ethical considerations in algorithmic management
  • Data-driven HR and talent management systems
  • Worker surveillance and monitoring through algorithms
  • Resistance and adaptation to algorithmic management
  • Regulatory and policy frameworks for AI in HR

Timeline

  • October 15, 2026: Extended abstract submission deadline

item.title: Entrepreneurship and the Creation of Decent Work for All
item.content:encoded:
Societal changes, environment, political and financial crises inevitably affect labor markets and the quality of employment. Recent pandemic and global political changes have only demonstrated how quickly one's employment and workplace situation can change. Among other factors, entrepreneurship could play a crucial role in the creation of decent work, especially in a volatile environment.

Understanding the relationship between entrepreneurship and working conditions is crucial for supporting policies and instruments which aim at more productive, decent work, fair wages, better access to the labor market, and improved job opportunities for all.

In order to fully represent this multifaceted topic, we would like to gather a spectrum of current perspectives in a single Collection, facilitating a better understanding of possibilities and ways of striving toward the goal of 'achieving full and productive employment and decent work for all' (SDG 8 of the U.N.).

Submissions to this collection may be research or review articles, depending on the individual journal guidelines. Each submission will undergo thorough and rigorous peer review in accordance with each journal's peer review editorial policy. Accepted articles will be published in the journal they were submitted to, as well as highlighted on this collection page.

Potential topics

  • Equal pay for work of equal value
  • Gender discrimination in employment
  • Immigration and employment
  • Labor shortages after COVID-19
  • Modern slavery and child labor
  • Labor policy
  • Entrepreneurial enterprises, SMEs, and family businesses
  • Global entrepreneurial firms: organization design, emerging conceptions in entrepreneurship (i.e. born globals), globalization's challenges and opportunities, cultural differences
  • Remote work
  • Opportunity entrepreneurship as a direct way to generate high quality employment
  • Measuring and dealing with positive and negative externalities of new businesses
